proposedTopics.title: Ethernaut wargame ladder
proposedTopics.description: The canonical entry-level wargame: Solidity levels deployed on Sepolia via a web UI, each a small vulnerable contract you must exploit through the console or your own scripts to progress. It is a fast way to turn the Phase-6 attack taxonomy into muscle memory — most levels map directly onto a bug class already studied.

proposedTopics.title: Damn Vulnerable DeFi v4 ladder
proposedTopics.description: Foundry-native, deliberately vulnerable DeFi protocols — 18 challenges in the current v4.1.0 release — each with a prompt, vulnerable contracts, and a Solidity test file where you code a solution without changing the initial or final conditions. V4 migrated the project to Foundry and added Curvy Puppet, Shards, Withdrawal, and a completely reworked Rewarder. It is the DeFi-specific complement to Ethernaut: flash loans, AMMs, oracles, governance, and cross-domain messaging.

proposedTopics.title: Real-exploit replay practice
proposedTopics.description: Wargames are synthetic; real incidents have real stakes and idiosyncrasies. DeFiHackLabs maintains runnable Foundry PoCs for historical incidents; DeFiVulnLabs currently catalogs 48 reusable vulnerability patterns; rekt.news and the BlockThreat newsletter build the pattern-recognition and incident-response intuition that reading code alone doesn't.

proposedTopics.title: Judged practice: CodeHawks First Flights
proposedTopics.description: First Flights are CodeHawks' beginner-scoped audit competitions — smaller codebases, real submissions, and professional judging so you learn what makes a finding survive review, not just 'I found a bug'. This is the graduation milestone for Phase 6: submit and get judged, not just solve a wargame.

proposedTopics.title: Additional wargame & campaign practice
proposedTopics.description: Optional extra reps once Ethernaut and DVD are done: ONLYPWNER is an EVM-focused challenge platform with difficulty-based scoring and a leaderboard, and Node Guardians runs gamified security quests and campaigns, including CTF-style replays of famous hacks on testnet. Neither is required for the milestone, but both keep the muscle warm.

proposedTopics.title: Ethernaut: fundamentals levels
proposedTopics.description: The first ten Ethernaut levels — Fallback, Fallout, CoinFlip, Telephone, Token, Delegation, Force, Vault, King, and Reentrancy — isolate bug classes from the attack taxonomy: weak authorization, constructor-name mistakes, predictable on-chain randomness, tx.origin authentication, pre-0.8 arithmetic, delegatecall storage effects, force-fed ETH, readable private storage, revert-based denial of service, and reentrancy. Solving them on the live Sepolia instance moves exploitation outside a Foundry test you control.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve Fallback, Fallout, CoinFlip, Telephone, Token, Delegation, Force, Vault, King, and Reentrancy on the public Ethernaut Sepolia instance; commit your attack scripts/contracts plus a one-paragraph writeup per level (which bug class, how you exploited it) to security/ethernaut/fundamentals/. Done when: all ten levels show 'You have completed this level!' and every level has a committed writeup.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut's first ten levels each isolate one bug class — name three and the taxonomy leaf each drills.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: e.g. Telephone → tx.origin authentication; Delegation → delegatecall storage collision; King → revert-based DoS on a push payment. Pitfall: solving the level in the console and then forgetting to write down WHICH bug class it was defeats the point — the ladder's value is pattern-matching back to the taxonomy, not just the flag.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Delegation: become the owner of the Delegation proxy without ever calling an owner-only function directly.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Delegation delegatecalls into Delegate.sol; call the proxy with calldata for Delegate's pwn() (its 4-byte selector) — delegatecall runs pwn()'s code in the proxy's storage context, so `owner = msg.sender` writes to the PROXY's owner slot.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — King: make yourself un-de-thronable so no one can ever become king again.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Submit a bid from a contract with no receive()/fallback (or one that reverts); the King contract's plain transfer/send refund to the ex-king fails, and if it doesn't handle that failure, the whole claim-kingship transaction reverts forever — a push-payment DoS.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does Motorbike's fix (removing the UUPS upgrade capability) work, and what made the level exploitable in the first place?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The Engine implementation could be initialized directly, making the caller its upgrader; under the level's historical semantics, upgradeToAndCall could delegatecall code that SELFDESTRUCTed the implementation and bricked proxies pointing at it. EIP-6780 now preserves an existing contract's code and storage unless SELFDESTRUCT runs in the same transaction that created it, so that old completion condition no longer follows on current Sepolia. The design fix remains disabling initializers on the implementation and authorizing upgrades correctly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Preservation: become the owner via a delegatecall to a library contract with a mismatched storage layout.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Preservation delegatecalls setFirstTime()/setSecondTime() into library contracts whose own storage layout has `uint storedTime` at slot 0 — but delegatecall writes into the CALLER's slot 0, which is `timeZone1Library`'s address. Overwrite that address with your own malicious library, then call setFirstTime again to run YOUR code, which writes to slot 2 (owner).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Puzzle Wallet: drain and take admin of a proxy whose admin slot collides with the wallet's storage.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: PuzzleProxy and PuzzleWallet share slots — pendingAdmin (proxy) aliases owner (wallet). Call proposeNewAdmin to set yourself as wallet owner, get whitelisted, then use multicall to call deposit() twice in one transaction (bypassing its 'no repeated calls' guard via nested calldata) so your recorded balance exceeds what you actually sent, withdraw it all, then setMaxBalance to overwrite the proxy's admin slot with your address.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does swapping back and forth on Ethernaut's Dex level let you drain one of its tokens, when the swap formula looks 'fair'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dex prices each swap from the current reserve ratio as amountOut = amountIn * toReserve / fromReserve, but it does not enforce a constant-product invariant. Alternating directions changes that quoted ratio each time; choose each input from the new reserves until the quote equals one entire reserve. Integer division rounds output down, so it is not a trader-favoring rounding exploit. Pitfall: this ISN'T the same bug as flash-loan spot manipulation — there's no external price oracle here, the pool's own naive formula is the whole vulnerability.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Dex Two: drain the pool using a token the pool doesn't actually hold.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: swap() never checks that from/to are the pool's real token1/token2 — deploy your own ERC-20, mint yourself an unlimited supply, and swap it in for the pool's real tokens at a favorable self-set rate.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Good Samaritan: trick the Wallet into giving away its entire balance instead of the small amount you requested.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Wallet.requestDonation() calls Coin.transfer(), catches a revert, and if the revert selector matches its own 'NotEnoughBalance' custom error it assumes the request was too big and sends the WHOLE remaining balance instead. Deploy a fake requester whose callback throws that exact custom error on a tiny request to trigger the full-balance payout.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is Ethernaut's Privacy level solvable even though the password is declared private?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: `private` only blocks OTHER CONTRACTS from reading the variable through Solidity syntax — it does nothing to hide the value on-chain. Storage is public data; read the slot directly with `cast storage <addr> <slot>` (or eth_getStorageAt), accounting for how the compiler packs a bytes32[3] array and a bool/uint8 into slots. Pitfall: 'private' is an access-control keyword for Solidity source, not an encryption primitive — never store real secrets in contract storage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Elevator: make a Building's isLastFloor() return two different answers to the same question in one call sequence.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Elevator's Building interface doesn't mark isLastFloor() as `view`, so nothing stops your implementation from returning false the first time it's called (letting goUp proceed) and true the second time (setting top=true) — an interface with no purity guarantee is not trustworthy just because its name implies a query.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Switch: flip the switch on when the contract's calldata check should forbid it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: flipSwitch(bytes) checks one fixed calldata word for turnSwitchOff's selector, but Solidity decodes the dynamic bytes argument from an attacker-controlled offset and later calls that decoded payload. Point the bytes offset past padding that contains the checked off selector, while the actual decoded payload begins with turnSwitchOn's selector; the check and execution then inspect different bytes.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Ethernaut: gas, calldata & bytecode puzzle levels
proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does calling GatekeeperTwo's gate from your contract's CONSTRUCTOR bypass its extcodesize(caller) == 0 check?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A contract's code isn't stored on-chain until its constructor finishes running, so extcodesize on an address still mid-construction reads 0 even though the address is (about to be) a contract — the check meant to reject 'must be an EOA' is fooled by timing, not identity. Pitfall: EXTCODESIZE==0 is NOT a reliable 'is this an EOA' test even outside this trick.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Ethernaut: gas, calldata & bytecode puzzle levels
proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Alien Codex: overwrite the owner slot by underflowing a dynamic array's length.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: In pre-0.8 Solidity, calling retract() on an empty bytes32[] codex decrements its length below zero, underflowing to 2^256-1 — the array now 'covers' all of storage. Compute the index that maps to slot 0 (owner) via the array's storage-layout formula (keccak256(slot) + index) and write your address there with revise().

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Ethernaut: gas, calldata & bytecode puzzle levels
proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut — Denial: make the contract's owner permanently unable to withdraw, without ever touching an owner-only function.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: withdraw() forwards a large/all remaining gas to a partner address you control via a low-level call with no gas cap and no success check; deploy a partner whose fallback burns all forwarded gas (e.g. an assembly infinite loop), so every withdraw() call runs out of gas before it can pay the real owner — a gas-griefing DoS on a push payment.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does Truster's flash-loan pool let you drain it without ever taking out a real loan?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: flashLoan() lets the borrower supply an ARBITRARY target address + calldata for the callback with no restriction on what it can call — call the pool itself, asking it to approve() your attacker contract for the full token balance, then just transferFrom it out; no repayment logic is ever exercised because a 0-amount 'loan' still runs your arbitrary call. Pitfall: an unrestricted flash-loan callback is equivalent to giving the borrower an arbitrary-call primitive on behalf of the pool — restrict the callback target/calldata, don't just check the loan is repaid.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Unstoppable: halt the flash-loan vault's flashLoan() for everyone, permanently.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The vault's flashLoan() asserts convertToShares(totalSupply) == balanceBefore as an invariant; directly transfer()-ing extra underlying tokens to the vault (bypassing deposit(), so shares don't mint) breaks that balance/shares invariant forever, reverting every future flash loan.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Side Entrance: drain a pool whose flash-loan callback lets you deposit.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Take a flash loan, and inside the callback deposit() the borrowed ETH back into the SAME pool — the pool's post-loan balance check passes (the ETH is physically back), but you've credited yourself an internal deposit balance you can withdraw() afterward for free. Cross-function reentrancy: flashLoan and deposit/withdraw share one balance with no unified guard.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the common root cause across the Puppet, Puppet V2, and Puppet V3 challenges, despite each using a different AMM version?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: All three price collateral off a swappable pool's CURRENT state (V1/V2 spot reserves, or a too-short/thin V3 TWAP window) — the attacker dumps the borrowed token into the pool to crater its price, borrows far more than the true-value collateral would allow, and (in the flash-loan variants) never needed their own capital. Pitfall: 'we upgraded to Uniswap V3 with a TWAP' is not automatically safe — a short window or a low-liquidity pair TWAP is still manipulable, just more expensive.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Puppet: drain a lending pool that prices collateral from a Uniswap spot pair.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dump your DVT tokens into the Uniswap pair to crater its spot price, then deposit a small amount of ETH as collateral (now 'worth' far more DVT at the crashed price) and borrow the pool's entire DVT balance.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Curvy Puppet: exploit a price source that reads a Curve pool's virtual price during a reentrant callback.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Trigger a Curve pool operation that sends ETH mid-transaction (e.g. remove_liquidity), and from the receiving callback, call into the consumer that reads get_virtual_price() BEFORE the pool's internal accounting has settled — borrow/liquidate against the transiently wrong price, matching the read-only-reentrancy pattern already studied.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does ABI Smuggling let an attacker bypass a permissioned function's access check without ever forging a valid selector?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The authorizer validates the FIRST 4 bytes of forwarded calldata (the function selector) against a permission list, but a downstream contract executes the FULL calldata including extra, attacker-crafted bytes appended or nested beyond what the selector-check inspected — the check and the execution disagree about what 'the call' actually is. Pitfall: validating a prefix of calldata (the selector) is not the same as validating the whole call; any encoding step between the check and the execution is an injection point.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Selfie: pass a malicious governance proposal using flash-loaned voting power.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Flash-borrow the voting token, delegate the borrowed balance to yourself so ERC20Votes.getVotes reports a majority, queue a proposal calling the pool's emergencyExit(recovery), then repay the loan. After the governance delay, execute the queued action. The v4.1 contract checks current voting power when an action is queued; it does not expose the old snapshot() flow. A safer design checks past votes from a block before the proposal transaction or otherwise prevents transient borrowed voting power.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Damn Vulnerable DeFi — Backdoor: steal the registration reward from wallets created for other beneficiaries.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The registry validates each new Safe's singleton, one beneficiary owner, threshold, and fallback handler, then transfers the reward into that wallet. Safe setup also permits a delegatecall to an arbitrary target. Put token.approve(player, reward) in that setup delegatecall; after the registry funds each otherwise-valid wallet, use transferFrom to move its reward to recovery. The bypass is initialization-time arbitrary execution, not a fake expected module.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does replaying an incident at its documented chain state matter, instead of writing a fresh toy contract with 'the same bug'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The real victim's bug is often entangled with deployed integrations, token quirks, oracle interfaces, and exact storage state that a simplified rewrite could accidentally fix or hide. Following the repository PoC's recorded chain, fork block, transaction, or local setup gives much stronger evidence that you reproduced that incident rather than a lookalike. Pitfall: not every DeFiHackLabs entry is a mainnet fork or uses one universal pre-exploit-block convention.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Replay a real reentrancy incident (e.g. an ERC-777/ERC-1155 hook-driven drain) from DeFiHackLabs at its documented chain state.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Find the incident's indexed PoC, run its documented command and chain/fork setup, and confirm the recorded exploit path and observed balance change. Then explain the smallest CEI or reentrancy-guard mitigation that closes that specific path; do not assume every incident runs on mainnet or at the block immediately before the exploit transaction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Replay a real oracle-manipulation incident from DeFiHackLabs (e.g. a spot-price or flash-loan-funded manipulation).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Run the selected incident's documented command and recorded chain/fork setup, confirm the PoC's price-moving sequence and observed victim balance change, then explain whether a sufficiently configured TWAP, independent oracle, or another incident-specific control would reject it. Do not substitute one generic pre-exploit-block recipe for the repository entry's actual setup.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference in what DeFiHackLabs and DeFiVulnLabs each teach, given they cover overlapping incidents?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: DeFiHackLabs teaches EXECUTION against a real, messy, specific deployed system (forked PoCs); DeFiVulnLabs teaches RECOGNITION — the minimal abstracted shape of the bug, stripped of one incident's specific noise, so you can spot the same pattern in a codebase that looks nothing like the original victim. Pitfall: doing only one of the two leaves a gap — pattern recognition without execution practice doesn't build the muscle to actually write a working exploit under contest time pressure, and vice versa.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Map DeFiVulnLabs's read-only-reentrancy and price-oracle-manipulation patterns to the exact 06b/06c leaves that cover them.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Read-only reentrancy pattern → 'Read-only reentrancy' and 'Read-only reentrancy into oracles'; price-manipulation patterns → 'Spot-price oracle manipulation', 'TWAP oracle manipulation', 'Flash-loan price manipulation' — note any DeFiVulnLabs pattern (e.g. a specific rebasing-token quirk) that doesn't already have a home leaf.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Real-exploit replays: rekt.news & BlockThreat incident intuition
proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is skimming 10 incident writeups a week different in kind from replaying one incident in Foundry, and why do you need both?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Breadth (rekt/BlockThreat) trains fast classification — recognizing 'this smells like a first-depositor inflation bug' from a headline-level description before digging in; depth (DeFiHackLabs replay) trains the actual exploit-writing muscle. An auditor needs both: breadth to triage what to look at first in a real codebase, depth to actually prove the finding. Pitfall: breadth without ever replaying anything produces false confidence — you recognize the shape but haven't proven you can exploit it under time pressure.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Real-exploit replays: rekt.news & BlockThreat incident intuition
proposedPrompts.promptText: Read this week's BlockThreat digest (or a recent rekt.news post-mortem) and classify the top incident by attack family.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Identify the root-cause category (reentrancy / access-control / oracle-price / arithmetic / business-logic / etc.), name the matching 06b/06c taxonomy leaf, and state the one design decision (a check, an invariant, a timelock) that would have prevented the loss.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: beginner audit contests
proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does competing in a real First Flight teach something Ethernaut/DVD wargames structurally can't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Wargames have ONE known bug and a clear win condition (drain the contract); a First Flight codebase may have zero, one, or several bugs of unknown location and severity, on a fixed clock, judged by a human against a rubric — you must decide what's worth reporting, not just whether you can exploit something. Pitfall: treating a First Flight like a wargame ('find THE bug') under-reports; treating a wargame like an audit ('write up every theoretical issue') over-reports — First Flights calibrate that judgment.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: beginner audit contests
proposedPrompts.promptText: Enter a CodeHawks First Flight contest and submit at least one finding before the contest closes.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Scope the codebase during the review window, write findings in CodeHawks' report format as you go (don't wait until the end), and submit before the deadline — late submissions aren't judged regardless of quality.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: writing a finding that survives judging
proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the most common reasons a technically-correct finding gets downgraded or rejected in CodeHawks judging?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: No runnable PoC (a claim without proof), severity asserted without justification against the actual impact + likelihood, an impact statement broader than what the PoC actually demonstrates, or duplicate/near-duplicate of an already-submitted finding. Pitfall: 'this could theoretically lead to X' without a PoC reads as speculation to a judge — always show the concrete path from bug to loss, even if the PoC is minimal.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks First Flights: writing a finding that survives judging
proposedPrompts.promptText: Rewrite a First Flight finding you submitted informally into the full CodeHawks report format and resubmit/record its verdict.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Use the current contest's live form rather than assuming one immutable template. Supply its required title, severity, and detailed description/reproduction fields; ground severity in impact and likelihood, keep within scope, add a runnable test when applicable, separate attacker/victim/protocol roles, and propose a specific mitigation.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks AI First Flights: standalone AI-graded practice
proposedPrompts.promptText: How do CodeHawks AI First Flights differ from the scheduled human-judged First Flights, and how should you use them?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: AI First Flights let you choose when to start, then give you one week and instant AI evaluation with no appeals; regular First Flights run on scheduled platform windows and proceed through professional judging and appeals. Use AI First Flights for fast iteration between regular competitions, not as a substitute for judged scope, duplication, and severity decisions.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: CodeHawks AI First Flights: standalone AI-graded practice
proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete one standalone CodeHawks AI First Flight practice audit end-to-end and act on the AI's grading.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pick an AI First Flight, review its codebase, submit your findings, and read the AI's instant grading; note every gap it flags (missing PoC, unjustified severity, vague impact) and record one concrete lesson to carry into your next real contest.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why keep doing wargame-style practice after finishing Ethernaut and DVD, instead of moving straight to real audits?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pattern-recognition speed and exploit-writing fluency both degrade without repetition, and a fixed, exhaustive ladder (Ethernaut/DVD) eventually runs out — ongoing platforms with a growing challenge set (ONLYPWNER, Node Guardians) keep the reps coming without waiting for a new CTF season. Pitfall: novelty-seeking across platforms without ever writing up WHAT was learned (unlike the taxonomy-mapping discipline in the required ladders) turns practice into pure entertainment — keep the one-line bug-class note per challenge.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve at least one ONLYPWNER challenge and record which bug class it drilled.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pick a challenge near your current level on the leaderboard's difficulty signal, solve it, and note the bug class (it will usually map to a 06b/06c taxonomy leaf) in security/campaigns/.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete a Node Guardians security-themed quest or campaign chapter.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Node Guardians' CTF-on-testnet mode replays famous hacks in a gamified quest chain — pick a security campaign, complete its chapters, and log the bug class(es) drilled in security/campaigns/.
